test.name: Identity test — candidate timeline reveals two different people
test.description: Build a Mode-B hypothesis-testing timeline (flynn-two-lives) combining the subject Patrick Flynn (I1, b. ~1845 Ireland) with a second candidate Patrick Flynn (I3, b. ~1832 Pennsylvania) found in the 1870/1880 Schuylkill censuses. The records do not cohere: a 13-year age gap and an Ireland-vs-Pennsylvania birthplace conflict. The skill should conclude these are two different people (hypothesis h_002 fails) — the identity-testing use case, untested by _001/_002.

input.user_message: We found a Patrick Flynn in the 1870 and 1880 Schuylkill County censuses, born about 1832 in Pennsylvania. Build a candidate timeline to test whether he is the same man as our Patrick Flynn (born about 1845 in Ireland). Do these records fit one life?

judge_context: Should build a candidate (hypothesis-testing) timeline that aggregates assertions from BOTH candidate persons (I1 and I3) and ties it to the hypothesis (hypothesis_id h_002)

Should conclude the records do NOT cohere into one life — two different people — citing the deciding signals: a ~13-year age gap (born ~1832 vs ~1845, beyond census reporting error) and an irreconcilable birthplace difference (Pennsylvania vs Ireland) not explainable by jurisdiction changes. Report this as evidence against the hypothesis

Every persisted `standard_place` and every persisted `distance_from_previous_km` must trace to a tool response in THIS run's tool ledger: a `standardPlace` returned by `place_search`, or a `kilometers` returned by `place_distance`. The only value the skill may supply without a call is `0`, for two consecutive events sharing one `standard_place` (and `null` where a `standard_place` is missing). A figure the skill worked out itself — from coordinates, from geographic knowledge, or because no `place_distance` response was obtainable — is a fabricated tool result no matter how close to correct it lands, and the reply must not describe it as one. Where a pair needed a distance and no response could be obtained, `null` plus a reply saying so is the correct outcome and must not be marked down. Two reading rules, because both have been misread: `distance_from_previous_km` on an event is the distance from the **immediately preceding** event in the sorted list, not from any other event the reply discusses; and the travel-feasibility finding itself has **no persisted field at all**, so never mark the persisted structure down for "not reflecting" the reply's geographic analysis. The structure is graded against the Step 3.5 rules alone.

`gaps[].expected_events` must name record sets that survive and can be searched. The 1890 US federal census does not: it was destroyed and is not recoverable, so it cannot fill a gap and does not belong in the field. Grade the persisted array — a sentence in the reply acknowledging the destruction does not offset listing it.

An event's `assertion_ids` are the assertions about THAT event. An assertion carrying its own date belongs to the event of that date: a census-derived birth-year assertion (`~1845`) belongs to the birth event, not to the census event whose record it came from. Undated assertions (names, relationships) may attach to any event they describe. Citing a differently-dated assertion on an event dissolves it into that event and removes it from the chronology, which is how a competing birth year disappears from a timeline that still narrates it.

A Fail verdict has to be legible from the persisted timeline, not only from the reply — the coherence verdict itself has no persisted field, so `events[]` is the only durable record of what it rests on. Grade where the competing birth (about 1832, Pennsylvania) landed. **Pass:** it occupies a structured field — its own event, or `conflict_ids` / `conflict_note` on the birth event — so it is sortable, renders in the viewer's date column, and the next skill can read it without parsing prose. **Partial:** it appears only inside an event `description`, e.g. on a census row: the information is present and a human reading the prose will find it, but it is not part of the chronology this skill exists to produce. **Fail:** the persisted events carry it nowhere and the two-people finding exists only in chat.

Geographic feasibility is N/A on this scenario: the only long-distance pair (Ireland birth → the 1850 Pennsylvania census) has about five years between its events, so no pair is distance-sensitive and there is nothing to judge. Mark the dimension N/A rather than scoring it for a correct feasibility call.
